expected_evidence: Geological: a discrete tephra/ash layer or volcanic glass shard horizon in Mexican lake, cave, or loess/paleosol sequences dated to ~12,000–11,000 BP, ideally geochemically fingerprinted to a specific Mexican volcanic center (e.g., trans-Mexican volcanic belt eruptions)

Geological/geochemical: anomalous concentrations of volcanic markers (sulfate spikes, glass shards, specific trace-element signatures) coinciding with the youngest-dryas-onset 'black mat' or extinction horizon
Material: megafaunal bone beds or kill/death assemblages stratigraphically capped or interbedded with ashfall deposits, showing a sudden extinction/disappearance horizon
Material: archaeological site abandonment layers or ash-covered occupation surfaces in central Mexico dated to the same window
Genetic (ancient DNA): a population bottleneck or extirpation signal in megafaunal (mammoth, horse, ground sloth) genomes from Mexican/North American samples dated near 12,000–11,000 BP

Astronomical/atmospheric proxies (less applicable to a purely volcanic actor, but sometimes reported): cosmic dust or platinum-group anomalies that would actually argue against a volcanic origin and for an impact origin, creating an internal inconsistency
Oral tradition: Indigenous Mesoamerican origin/disaster narratives referencing fire, darkness, or ash from the sky
Iconographic: rock art or petroglyphs depicting eruption events or mass animal death (very unlikely to survive/be attributable this far back)
Model-prior: known large-magnitude Pleistocene-Holocene boundary eruptions in the Mexican volcanic belt with dated tephra correlated to megafaunal decline
response.rationale: The interval (-12000 to -11001) sits at the Pleistocene/Holocene transition, closest to the 'younger-dryas' period bucket rather than 'upper-paleolithic' proper, though both are similar. For this hypothesis the decisive evidence kinds are geological (tephra/ash geochemistry, sediment horizons) and material (bone beds, extinction layers), which have relatively good survivability at this age (geological ~0.65, material ~0.35 per the younger-dryas row) because volcanic ash layers and stratified sediment cores in Mexican lake basins and caves are known to persist for tens of thousands of years and are routinely sampled by tephrochronologists. Genetic evidence (ancient DNA bottleneck signals, ~0.3) is moderately plausible but requires well-preserved megafaunal remains, which are rarer in tropical/subtropical Mexican contexts than in temperate/arctic settings. Textual (0.0), linguistic (0.05), oral_tradition (0.1), and iconographic (0.1) evidence are essentially non-recoverable or unreliable this far back, consistent with the near-zero detectability scores for a pre-literate period. Note an internal tension in the hypothesis itself: 'impact-ejecta-fallout' is the mechanism conventionally invoked for the Younger Dryas *extraterrestrial impact* hypothesis (e.g., cosmic dust, platinum-group anomalies), not for volcanic eruptions, which instead produce tephra/sulfate signatures — this actor/mechanism mismatch is a model-prior (unverified, recalled from training) concern and somewhat undermines the hypothesis's internal coherence rather than its detectability per se. On balance, if a genuine large Mexican eruption causally linked to megafaunal extinction had occurred in this window, tephra and extinction-horizon evidence plausibly could have survived and been detected via existing tephrochronology and paleontological sampling; the absence of such a well-documented, geochemically matched eruption in the literature (to my knowledge) is more consistent with the hypothesis being unsupported/speculative than with evidence having been destroyed. I set the adjustment (0.45) below the raw geological score to reflect that the strongest evidence class (geological) is offset by weaker material/genetic support and the actor-mechanism inconsistency, while still crediting real survivability of ashfall/sediment records for this period.
